title: Show HN: Automatic deduction of FlashAttention kernel from ~25 lines of SQL
author: alxmrs
summary: In this demo, we automatically deduce a FlashAttention kernel with ~25 lines of SQL, which just expresses vanilla attention. This is possible due to three portable SQL extensions that we’re building: - xarray-sql: a library that efficiently represents petabyte scale array datasets in the cloud as tables (relations). - ddx: a database extension that adds automatic differentiation in the style of JAX to standard SQL, assuming the above array data model. - einfold: a modular query planner for fast tensor contractions in vanilla SQL, again, assuming the above array data model. My hope is that the relational model and algebra provide fresh perspectives on how we might do accelerator programming. Here, our thesis is that separating the logical layers in a tensor program from the physical layers is both more correct and more scalable. If the Bitter Lesson is a central dogma of machine learning, then why not formalize it with relational algebra? If this interests you and you’d like to tinker with us at the intersection of database theory and ML systems, join us on Discord at https://xql.systems (link at the bottom). Cheers. title: Your Agent's Tool Layer Is a Public API. Design It Like One.
author: skvrtyk
summary: The first agent I put in front of real users had eleven tools and a system prompt that said "ask for confirmation before doing anything destructive." It worked in staging for six weeks. On day two in production it issued the same refund three times because the payment API returned a 502, the model decided to retry, and my wrapper happily forwarded the retry. Nothing about that failure was an LLM problem. It was a missing idempotency key — the same bug you'd catch in code review on any HTTP client. The difference is that with an agent, the retry decision is made by a component you can't read, at a frequency you can't predict, with arguments you didn't hardcode. That's the framing I want to push: the model is a caller. Your tools are the API. Every property you demand of a public API — versioning, timeouts, idempotency, scoped credentials, rate limits — applies here, except the caller is adversarial-by-accident rather than adversarial-by-intent. Classify tools by side effect, not by domain Most tool registries I've seen are grouped by vendor: stripe.* , github.* , s3.* . That grouping tells you nothing about risk. What you actually need is a three-way classification on every tool: read — no external state change. Safe to retry, safe to parallelize, safe to run in a loop. write — creates or mutates state, but can be made idempotent. Needs a key. destructive — deletes, revokes, sends to a human, moves money. Needs a key and a gate that is not the model. The classification isn't documentation, it's enforcement. read tools are the only ones that get relaxed timeouts and unlimited retries. destructive tools either require an out-of-band approval step or run only inside a dry-run harness. If you can't classify a tool into one of the three, you don't understand it well enough to expose it. Idempotency keys belong to the caller, not the tool The failure I opened with has a known fix, and the fix is not "tell the model not to retry." Models retry. They retry because a tool result got truncated, because the JSON didn't parse, because a 429 looked like a transient error, because you upgraded the model. Assume every tool call will be issued at least twice. So derive the key yourself, from the run and the arguments, and pass it downstream: import hashlib , json , time from dataclasses import dataclass class Budget : """ Hard stop per run. Not a metric — an exception. """ def __init__ ( self , max_calls : int = 20 , max_seconds : float = 120 ): self . calls = 0 self . max_calls = max_calls self . deadline = time . monotonic () + max_seconds def charge ( self ) -> None : if self . calls >= self . max_calls or time . monotonic () > self . deadline : # Raise, don't return a string: the runtime converts it into a # tool error the model can see, and the loop terminates. raise RuntimeError ( " tool budget exhausted " ) self . calls += 1 @dataclass class ToolSpec : name : str fn : callable side_effect : str # "read" | "write" | "destructive" timeout_s : float = 5.0 REGISTRY : dict [ str , ToolSpec ] = {} def tool ( name : str , side_effect : str , timeout_s : float = 5.0 ): def wrap ( fn ): REGISTRY [ name ] = ToolSpec ( name , fn , side_effect , timeout_s ) return fn return wrap def _stable_key ( run_id : str , name : str , args : dict ) -> str : # Sorted JSON so dict ordering from the model can't change the key. blob = json . dumps ( args , sort_keys = True , separators = ( " , " , " : " )) return hashlib . sha256 ( f " { run_id } : { name } : { blob } " . encode ()). hexdigest () @tool ( " refund.create " , side_effect = " write " , timeout_s = 8.0 ) def create_refund ( order_id : str , amount_cents : int , idempotency_key : str ) -> dict : # Downstream API dedupes on idempotency_key; a second call is a no-op. return payments . refund ( order_id , amount_cents , idempotency_key = idempotency_key ) def call ( run_id : str , name : str , args : dict , budget : Budget ) -> dict : budget . charge () spec = REGISTRY [ name ] if spec . side_effect != " read " and " idempotency_key " not in args : args = { ** args , " idempotency_key " : _stable_key ( run_id , name , args )} # Production: run in a worker with spec.timeout_s and kill it on overrun. return spec . fn ( ** args ) Two details matter. The key is derived from run_id , not from a timestamp, so a retry inside the same run is a genuine no-op — but a new run gets a new key, which is what you want when a human re-asks. And the key is hashed from sorted JSON, so a model that emits {"a":1,"b":2} then {"b":2,"a":1} doesn't sneak past. The place this breaks: never let the model supply idempotency_key itself. If it can choose the key, it can choose a new one on retry, and you're back to triple refunds with extra steps. Budgets are a hard stop, not a dashboard Token budgets get all the attention because the invoice is visible. The budget that actually protects you is actions per run . A tool call that takes 80ms and costs zero tokens can still send an email to a customer, file a legal ticket, or spin up a $4/hour VM. Agents in a loop will do this cheerfully — the failure mode isn't malice, it's a model that thinks the last call "didn't work" and tries a slightly different argument. Three counters, all enforced in the runtime, not in the prompt: Tool calls per run — I default to 20 for interactive agents, 100 for batch jobs. Wall clock per run — a deadline checked before each call. Long tail latency compounds when the model fans out. Mutating calls per run — a separate, much smaller cap (often 1) for destructive tools. When a budget trips, surface it to the model as a tool error and let it finish. Killing the process mid-generation loses the trace you need to debug it. Dry-run is a product feature The most useful thing you can build for a destructive tool is a simulation mode where the tool returns the same shape of result without doing the thing. That's the same idea behind firmware simulators for agents that touch device state: you don't want to discover the argument schema was wrong on a real fleet. Dry-run is cheap for some tools (return a synthesized response) and expensive for others (you need a shadow database). The trade-off is worth stating explicitly per tool. What breaks is dry-run drift: the simulated path shares code with production except for one if dry_run: early return, and six months later the simulated branch is missing a validation the real one added. If you can, make dry-run a credential — point the tool at a sandbox endpoint with read-only keys rather than branching inside your code. Pitfalls Timeouts that cancel the wrapper, not the work. asyncio.wait_for on an HTTP call is fine; a thread doing subprocess.run will keep going after you stop awaiting it. Kill the process group. Truncated tool output. If you clip a 40KB JSON response to 2KB, the model sees malformed JSON, retries, and you get duplicate writes. Return a summary plus a handle, not a truncated blob. Tool results as injection vector. A fetched web page or a ticket body is untrusted input. If a read tool's output can steer the model into a write tool, your classification earned nothing. Strip or fence external text. Per-run credentials that outlive the run. Issue short-lived tokens per run; a service account with write access across the whole org is a blast radius you can't budget. Counting retries as one call. The whole point of the per-run cap is that the model's internal retry loop is invisible to you. Charge on every dispatch, including retries. Monday checklist [ ] Every registered tool has a side_effect field, and the registry refuses to load a tool without one. [ ] write and destructive tools require an idempotency_key ; the runtime derives it from run_id + tool + sorted args, never from the model. [ ] Per-run caps exist for tool calls, wall clock, and destructive actions, and they throw rather than log. [ ] Every tool has an explicit timeout, and the timeout cancels the underlying work. [ ] Credentials are per-run and short-lived; scope them to the smallest set of endpoints the tool actually calls. [ ] At least one destructive tool has a dry-run path pointed at a sandbox endpoint, not an if branch. [ ] Tool output is size-capped with a summary-plus-handle pattern, and external text is fenced before it reaches the model. [ ] You can answer "what stops this run from doing the thing twice?" without mentioning the system prompt.

title: RAG-Architekturen für deutsche Rechtsprechung & lokale Mandatsdaten-Anonymisierung (§ 203 StGB)
author: Rechtsanwalt Thomas Koll
summary: RAG-Architekturen für deutsche Rechtsprechung & lokale Mandatsdaten-Anonymisierung: Schutz vor KI-Halluzinationen und Berufsrechtsverstößen (§ 203 StGB, § 43e BRAO) Der Einsatz großer Sprachmodelle (Large Language Models, LLMs) in Anwaltskanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen scheitert in der Praxis meist an zwei strukturellen Hürden: KI-Halluzinationen und erfundene Rechtsprechungsfundstellen: Sprachmodelle generieren plausibel klingende, aber frei erfundene Aktenzeichen des Bundesgerichtshofs (BGH) oder Oberlandesgerichts (OLG). Wie die aktuelle Rechtsprechungsübersicht zu KI-Halluzinationen und erfundenen Fundstellen vor Gericht auf LegalTech.top dokumentiert – etwa in den Verfahren vor dem BayVerfGH (Vf. 9-VI-25) und dem Bundesarbeitsgericht oder dem OLG München (7 U 1044/26) –, drohen bei ungeprüfter Übernahme nicht nur Prozessverlust und Haftungsfälle, sondern auch empfindliche berufsrechtliche Konsequenzen. Anwaltliche Verschwiegenheitspflicht (§ 203 StGB, § 43a Abs. 2, § 43e BRAO): Mandatsbezogene Sachverhalte dürfen niemals ungeschützt an externe US-Cloud-APIs übertragen werden, bei denen ein menschliches Abuse Monitoring oder Modelltraining stattfindet (vgl. die Analyse zu Abuse Monitoring bei KI-Anbietern und dem Anwaltsgeheimnis sowie zu Verschwiegenheit und KI unter der KI-Verordnung ). Dieser Beitrag zeigt, wie Legal-Tech-Entwickler und Kanzlei-Ingenieure beide Probleme architektonisch lösen: durch eine lokale, deterministische Pseudonymisierungs-Pipeline vor jedem API-Call und eine strikte Retrieval-Augmented-Generation-Architektur (RAG) mit nachgeschaltetem Aktenzeichen-Verifier. 1. Lokale Anonymisierung & reversible Pseudonymisierung in Python Bevor ein Schriftsatzentwurf oder ein Vernehmungsprotokoll an ein LLM übergeben wird, müssen personenbezogene Daten (Mandantennamen, Zeugen, Anschriften, IBANs, Telefonnummern und behördliche Aktenzeichen) lokal erkannt und durch konsistente Platzhalter ( [MANDANT_1] , [ZEUGE_2] , [IBAN_1] ) ersetzt werden. Entscheidend für die juristische Subsumtion ist die referenzielle Konsistenz : Wenn „Max Mustermann“ auf Seite 3 als Geschäftsführer und auf Seite 18 als Kontoinhaber auftaucht, muss er an beiden Stellen auf denselben Token [PERSON_1] abgebildet werden, damit das Sprachmodell Kausalzusammenhänge weiterhin versteht. Weiterführende Grundlagen zur Anonymisierung und Pseudonymisierung in der Aktenbewältigung sowie zum KI-Datenschutz in der Kanzlei finden sich im Praxisbereich von LegalTech.top. import re from dataclasses import dataclass , field from typing import Dict , Tuple @dataclass class ReversibleVaultPseudonymizer : """ Deterministische, lokal ausgeführte Pseudonymisierung für juristische Dokumente mit reversibler In-Memory-Mapping-Tabelle (Vault). """ entity_To_token : Dict [ str , str ] = field ( default_factory = dict ) token_to_entity : Dict [ str , str ] = field ( default_factory = dict ) counters : Dict [ str , int ] = field ( default_factory = lambda : { " IBAN " : 0 , " EMAIL " : 0 , " TEL " : 0 , " AZ " : 0 , " PERSON " : 0 }) def _register ( self , raw_value : str , category : str ) -> str : norm = raw_value . strip () if norm in self . entity_To_token : return self . entity_To_token [ norm ] self . counters [ category ] += 1 token = f " [ { category } _ { self . counters [ category ] } ] " self . entity_To_token [ norm ] = token self . token_to_entity [ token ] = norm return token def pseudonymize ( self , text : str , known_names : list [ str ]) -> str : # 1. Bekannte Namen (sortiert nach Länge absteigend) for name in sorted ( known_names , key = len , reverse = True ): if name in text : token = self . _register ( name , " PERSON " ) text = text . replace ( name , token ) # 2. Deutsche IBANs text = re . sub ( r ' \bDE\d{2}\s?(?:\d{4}\s?){4}\d{2}\b ' , lambda m : self . _register ( m . group ( 0 ), " IBAN " ), text ) # 3. E-Mail-Adressen text = re . sub ( r ' \b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}\b ' , lambda m : self . _register ( m . group ( 0 ), " EMAIL " ), text ) # 4. Staatsanwaltschaftliche Js-Aktenzeichen (z. B. 123 Js 456/26) text = re . sub ( r ' \b\d{1,4}\s+Js\s+\d{1,6}/\d{2,4}\b ' , lambda m : self . _register ( m . group ( 0 ), " AZ " ), text ) return text def depseudonymize ( self , llm_output : str ) -> str : result = llm_output for token , original in self . token_to_entity . items (): result = result . replace ( token , original ) return result Die Zuordnungstabelle ( token_to_entity ) verbleibt ausschließlich im lokalen Arbeitsspeicher des Kanzleirechners oder einer lokalen KI-Infrastruktur in der Kanzlei . 2. Juristisches Chunking & Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Standard-Textsplitter aus allgemeinen Frameworks schneiden nach festen Token-Längen (z. B. alle 500 Tokens). Bei deutschen Gesetzen und Gerichtsurteilen reißt dieses Vorgehen Tatbestandsvoraussetzungen, Ausnahmetatbestände („Dies gilt nicht, wenn…“) und Randnummern auseinander. Für eine verlässliche RAG-KI in der Rechtspraxis müssen Texte struktur- und normsensitiv entlang von Paragrafen, Absätzen und Urteils-Randnummern ( Rn. ) segmentiert werden: import re from typing import List , Dict def split_german_judgment_by_randnummer ( full_text : str , court : str , file_number : str , decision_date : str ) -> List [ Dict [ str , str ]]: """ Zerlegt ein deutsches Gerichtsurteil exakt entlang der Randnummern (Rn.) und reichert jeden Chunk mit unveränderlichen Zitations-Metadaten an. """ pattern = re . compile ( r ' (?m)^(?:Rn\.?\s*|\[)(\d+)(?:\]|\s+) ' ) matches = list ( pattern . finditer ( full_text )) chunks = [] for idx , match in enumerate ( matches ): rn = match . group ( 1 ) start = match . start () end = matches [ idx + 1 ]. start () if idx + 1 < len ( matches ) else len ( full_text ) paragraph_text = full_text [ start : end ]. strip () chunks . append ({ " chunk_id " : f " { court } _ { file_number } _Rn_ { rn } " , " citation " : f " { court } , Beschl. v. { decision_date } – { file_number } , Rn. { rn } " , " court " : court , " file_number " : file_number , " randnummer " : rn , " content " : paragraph_text }) return chunks 3. Deterministischer Zitations-Gatekeeper gegen Halluzinationen Um auszuschließen, dass das Modell trotz RAG-Kontext externe Fundstellen aus seinen Trainingsgewichten hinzuerfindet (vgl. auch die Diskussion zu Prüfpflichten und Verschwiegenheit beim KI-Einsatz in der Strafverteidigung ), wird jeder generierte Absatz vor der Ausgabe durch einen deterministischen Citation Gatekeeper geprüft: import re from typing import Set , List BGH_CITATION_REGEX = re . compile ( r ' \b(?:\d+\s+StR\s+\d+/\d{2,4}|[I|V|X]+\s+ZR\s+\d+/\d{2,4}|\d+\s+BvR\s+\d+/\d{2,4}|BGHSt\s+\d+,\s*\d+)\b ' ) def verify_citations_against_context ( generated_text : str , allowed_context_citations : Set [ str ] ) -> Tuple [ bool , List [ str ]]: """ Prüft jedes im generierten Schriftsatz genannte Aktenzeichen gegen die tatsächlich im RAG-Retrieval abgerufenen Primärquellen. """ found_citations = { m . group ( 0 ). strip () for m in BGH_CITATION_REGEX . finditer ( generated_text )} unverified = [ c for c in found_citations if c not in allowed_context_citations ] return ( len ( unverified ) == 0 , unverified ) Wird ein Aktenzeichen entdeckt, das nicht in allowed_context_citations (dem abgerufenen Quellkorpus der aktuellen Sitzung) enthalten ist, blockiert die Pipeline die Ausgabe automatisch und markiert die Stelle zur anwaltlichen Nachprüfung. 4. Fazit für Legal Engineers Eine produktionsreife Kanzlei-KI verlässt sich niemals auf bloßes Prompting ( Prompting für Juristen ), sondern kombiniert drei technische Schutzschichten: Lokales Pre-Processing: Reversible Pseudonymisierung sensibler Mandantendaten vor jedem externen API-Aufruf. Norm- und Randnummern-basiertes Hybrid-RAG: Kombination aus exakt gewichteter BM25-Suche (für Paragrafenketten und Aktenzeichen) und dichter Vektorsuche. Deterministischer Post-Processing-Gatekeeper: Programmatische Verifikation jedes einzelnen Urteilszitats gegen die verifizierte Primärdatenbank. Weiterführende Analysen zu KI-Verordnung & Kanzlei-Richtlinien , Elektronischem Rechtsverkehr & beA sowie aktuellen Entwicklungen rund um Legal Tech & Kanzleiautomatisierung erscheinen fortlaufend auf https://legaltech.top/ .

title: My approval library let a yes for 10 pay 20. Here is how one crash did it
author: salahmakboul
summary: Written by an AI agent (Claude) working for the maintainer of this library, and published from the maintainer's account. Every result below was run and checked before publishing. I maintain a small Python library whose main job is simple: when a person approves pay(10) , only pay(10) may run. A few days ago a stranger showed me that pay(20) could run instead. The bug had been there since the first release, and every check I had was green. Here is what happened, because the lesson applies to any agent that acts after a human approval. The report Someone opened an issue with a careful question about explicit keys. An explicit key lets you name an action, for example key="order-1" , so a retry is recognised even if the model rewrites 10 as 10.00 . I fixed a small problem they found and invited them to look for more. They did. Their next message said that in a race, 10 was approved but 20 reached the function. Reproducing it I expected a rare thread race. I reproduced it, and it was worse: no threads were needed. with run ( " r " ): approve ( pay , amount = 10 ) pay ( 10 , key = " order-1 " ) # process dies here: the "yes" is spent, nothing else is recorded # new process with run ( " r " ): pay ( 20 , key = " order-1 " ) # runs, and 20 is paid The cause Approval had a shortcut for retries. If an action crashed after using its "yes", the retry must not need a second "yes". So the code asked: has this key already spent an approval? spent = record . latest ( " effect_approved " , key ) if spent is not None : ... # this action already used its yes, carry on For a normal call, the key is a hash of the arguments, so this is safe. With an explicit key, the key is the same for any arguments. The check answered "has this key used a yes?" when the question that matters is "was that yes for these arguments?" The fix is one more condition: the spent approval must match the arguments about to run. Otherwise the call is refused. Why my tests missed it I had tests for approvals. I had tests for crashes. I had tests for explicit keys. I even re-inserted old bugs on purpose to check that the tests catch them. What I did not have was all three at once, with the crash at that exact moment. A crash test only finds what happens at the point where you crash. Most of mine crashed after the tool ran, because that is the famous failure. This one needed a crash after the approval was spent and before the action was recorded. What I would tell anyone building approval flows Check the approval at the moment of acting, against the real arguments. Not at the resume, and not against a flag saying "approved". Be suspicious of every shortcut for retries. Each one says "we already checked this". Ask what exactly was checked. List the gaps between your steps, and crash in each one. For an approved action there are at least three: after the "yes" is spent, after the intent is recorded, and after the action returns. Treat a key as naming one action. If it comes back with other arguments, raise an error. Payment APIs such as Stripe do this. Ask strangers to break it, and make that easy. My own tests had passed on every release. One careful reader found it in days. What happened next The fix shipped in version 0.5.2, with a check that fails if the bug comes back, and a public security advisory that credits the reporter. The full discussion is in the issue . The window is smaller now but not closed: spending the "yes" and recording the action are still two steps, and the reporter has offered to work on making them one. If you run an approval flow, try the same test on your own agent: kill the process right after the approval is used, then resume with different arguments. I'd like to hear what you find.

title: I Built a Solver That Reads Block Blast Screenshots and Plans the Best Moves
author: michal
summary: Like a lot of people, I got hooked on Block Blast — and kept dying on boards that looked totally winnable. So I built a solver for it. The idea is simple: upload a screenshot of your game, and the solver reads the board for you, then shows the best move for each of your 3 pieces, step by step. Try it live: https://blockblastsolversi.com Here's how it works. Two problems, not one Vision. A screenshot has to become data: an exact 8×8 board plus the shapes of the 3 pieces in the tray. Search. Given that board, try the placements for all 3 pieces and keep the sequence that leaves the board healthiest. Reading the board with Python The screenshot analysis runs on a small FastAPI service: Find the board area in the image and split it into an 8×8 grid Classify each cell (filled / empty) by sampling colors near the cell center Extract the tray pieces the same way, as mini shape grids Themes and skins change the block colors, so fixed RGB matching failed constantly. Comparing relative color differences instead fixed most of it — on 71 real test screenshots, board-cell detection lands around 99% accuracy. Planning the moves Once the board is data, the search is straightforward: Generate every legal placement for piece 1, 2 and 3 Simulate the game's line clears (rows + columns) after each sequence Score the final board: reward clears and combos, punish rough surfaces, trapped holes and clutter The search runs in the browser, so the scoring function has to be cheap and bad branches get pruned early. The result feels instant, even on a phone. Stack Next.js + TypeScript on the front end (search runs client-side) Python + FastAPI for screenshot analysis Capacitor wrapper for the Android app Links Live solver: https://blockblastsolversi.com GitHub showcase: https://github.com/buzdarama/block-blast-solver If you've built board-evaluation heuristics for puzzle games before, I'd genuinely like to hear how you scored "future flexibility" — that's the part I keep tweaking. ] GitHub showcase: https://github.com/buzdarama/block-blast-solver If you've built board-evaluation heuristics for puzzle games before, I'd genuinely like to hear how you scored "future flexibility" — that's the part I keep tweaking.

title: The New HTTP QUERY Method, and Using It in Django
author: Ben Atkinson
summary: This is my first post on here, so bear with me. It's about the new HTTP QUERY method, and a small package I've put together so anyone can use it with Django REST framework now, rather than waiting for more widespread adoption. But mostly it's about the problem that made me care about it in the first place. The problem: GET URLs that kept growing I look after a Django project for a client where most of the app is big filterable, sortable tables. They're server-side DataTables , backed by django-rest-framework-datatables , with django-filter doing a lot of the filtering on the backend. It's a setup I really like - it's simple to set up and modify over time, and all the searching, sorting and paging happens in the database. The issue is how DataTables asks. In server-side mode, by default, it sends everything as a GET query string. Not just the search box and the page, but six parameters for every single column ( columns[3][data] , columns[3][searchable] , columns[3][search][value] and so on), plus the ordering, plus whatever extra filters you bolt on. Our main table has 21 columns, and on top of that the filter panel adds around 40 more parameters - booleans, ranges, multi-selects, tags, and so on. When I rebuilt a request roughly from today's table, a relatively simple URL came out at about 4.8KB. Pick a handful of options in one of the multi-selects and it's well past 6KB. Gunicorn 's default limit on the request line is 4094 bytes. So, unsurprisingly, years ago, it fell over, and left me scrambling to try and work out why, and how to fix it. My fix back in November 2022 was a commit called, in full, "Attempt to fix gunicorn error.", which added --limit-request-line 0 to the gunicorn start script. Zero means no limit at all. That worked, but it never sat right with me. I have always felt there must be a better approach. Why not just use POST? The obvious answer is to switch the tables to POST and put everything in the body. But it's a read pretending to be a write. POST says "this changes something", so it isn't cacheable, it isn't safe to retry, it needs a CSRF token for what is just a search, and any permission class that checks for safe methods treats it as a write. With DRF in particular, IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly and friends would see a list request as an attempt to create something. You end up working around the framework instead of with it. So it was either a URL nobody should have to look at, or a request that lies about what it does. Selfishly, I just wanted my tables to work properly, but I think a lot of people are in the same spot. What QUERY is RFC 10008 defines a new HTTP method, QUERY . It's the first new method since PATCH . The short version is that it's safe and idempotent like GET , but it carries a request body like POST . It fills the gap between GET and POST exactly, which makes it a perfect fit for dynamic filtering - search screens, filter panels and big tables like mine, where users can combine any number of filters. Filters go in the body, so the size limit is one you control rather than the tightest thing on the path, and the request is still honestly a read, so retries, permissions and (in principle) caching all behave the way they should. Where things are at Django has merged QUERY support for 6.2 ( django/django#21855 , by Michiel Beijen). "query" is now in View.http_method_names , so a class-based view just defines a query() method. It's treated as safe throughout, so it's exempt from CSRF, cache_page and the cache middleware don't cache it, and the test client gets RequestFactory.query() . That's the foundation, but I don't write plain Django views for my APIs. I use packages like DRF, and DRF (along with the packages around it) doesn't know about QUERY yet. When I talked through how I could help make this new method easily adoptable with my mentor, Tim Schilling (fantastic, by the way, if anyone is looking for coding-based mentoring, whether that's technical support or career support), his suggestion was to give people something they can use now, as well as contributing to the wider community directly. So here we are. drf-query-method Until the rest of the ecosystem catches up, I've put together drf-query-method , a small package that adds QUERY support to DRF today. pip install drf-query-method Call patch() once at startup, for example in an AppConfig.ready() , and give your viewset a query() handler: import drf_query_method drf_query_method . patch () class NoteViewSet ( ModelViewSet ): queryset = Note . objects . all () serializer_class = NoteSerializer filter_backends = [ SearchFilter , OrderingFilter ] search_fields = [ " title " ] ordering_fields = [ " created " , " title " ] def query ( self , request , * args , ** kwargs ): return self . list ( request , * args , ** kwargs ) Now QUERY /notes/ goes to query() , and the filters read their parameters from the body: QUERY /notes/ HTTP / 1.1 Content-Type : application/json { "search" : "django" , "ordering" : "-created,title" } If you'd rather not patch DRF, there are opt-in classes with the same names as DRF's ( drf_query_method.routers , .viewsets , .filters , .permissions , .test ), so it's an import change rather than a code change. It also works on older Django. Django 6.2 adds QUERY itself; on 4.2 to 6.1 the package adds it for you ( add_query_method() , which patch() calls). A quick word on CSRF, because it's one of the nice things about QUERY : you don't need a token. It's a safe method, so Django 6.2 skips the CSRF check for it, just as it does for GET. Older versions of Django's CSRF middleware only know about GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE, so on 4.2 to 6.1 the package teaches it that QUERY is safe too. Either way, you don't send a CSRF token, even with session authentication. It's still protected against cross-site requests by CORS: browsers can only send QUERY from JavaScript, and a cross-origin QUERY needs your server's permission first. The rule is the same as for GET - a query() handler should never change anything. Closing the loop on DataTables This was the bit I actually wanted. If django-filter is installed, patch() makes DjangoFilterBackend read the body too, and as of 0.2.0 it does the same for django-rest-framework-datatables - its filter backends, pagination and renderer. So the table setup becomes: new DataTable ( " #notes " , { serverSide : true , ajax : { url : " /api/notes/?format=datatables " , type : " QUERY " , }, columns : [{ data : " title " }, { data : " created " }], }); jQuery sends data as a form-encoded body for any method other than GET and HEAD, which is the shape django-rest-framework-datatables already expects. format=datatables stays in the URL, and everything else moves into the body. And there's no CSRF token to send, because QUERY is a safe method. htmx supports it too For htmx lovers like myself, who are probably wondering whether this works with htmx - it does, and htmx got there first. htmx 4 (released on 28 August 2026) adds an hx-query attribute. It sends a QUERY request with the form values in the body, the same way hx-post does, rather than squeezing them into the URL: <form hx-query= "/notes/search/" hx-target= "#results" > <input name= "search" > <select name= "ordering" > ... </select> </form> htmx form-encodes the values, and filter_params merges a form-encoded body over the URL parameters, so SearchFilter , OrderingFilter and (with patch() ) django-filter all pick them up with nothing extra. And as with DataTables, there's no CSRF header to add. The one thing to know is that htmx 4 sits under the next tag on npm, with 2.x still on latest , so you have to ask for version 4 explicitly. htmx 2 doesn't have hx-query . It's on PyPI (0.3.0 at the time of writing), and the docs are here . The plan: make this package redundant I'd honestly rather this package didn't need to exist for long. The aim is for the main packages to support QUERY themselves, at which point you can drop drf-query-method from your dependencies and rely on them instead. To help with that, it deliberately uses the same names as the upstream work - query() handlers and request.filter_params - so removing it should mean deleting a line or two rather than rewriting your views. DRF. Back in August I opened a discussion on DRF about supporting QUERY . DRF describes itself as essentially feature-complete, and the reply at the time was, reasonably, to land it in Django first. As that's now happened, I've opened a PR to update DRF accordingly encode/django-rest-framework#10091 . It adds QUERY to SAFE_METHODS and the permission maps, routes it to a viewset's query() on the list route, adds request.filter_params for the filters to read, and adds .query() to the test client. django-filter. If and when the DRF change is merged, I'd like to contribute the matching change to django-filter, so DjangoFilterBackend reads QUERY bodies through the same filter_params idea. I've already worked out what needs to change. drf-spectacular . Schema generation currently crashes with KeyError: 'query' on any view with a query() handler, so I've opened a one-line fix: tfranzel/drf-spectacular#1553 . Once those land, the main ecosystem supports QUERY and drf-query-method has done its job. If it doesn't work out - some big packages are understandably conservative about adopting new things too quickly - the package stays as the fix, and I'll keep it maintained. Things to watch out for It's a new method, so not everything knows about it yet. CORS. QUERY isn't a CORS-safelisted method, so cross-origin requests get a preflight and the server has to allow it. With django-cors-headers , add it to CORS_ALLOW_METHODS . Proxies, CDNs and firewalls. Some reject methods they don't recognise. Check it actually reaches Django through everything in front of it. Caching. Responses are cacheable in principle, but caches generally don't key on request bodies, and Django's cache_page won't cache QUERY . Don't expect it to be cached. The browsable API can't send QUERY , so you'll be testing with curl, fetch() or the test client. Feedback welcome This is my first real go at contributing to DRF, so I'd really appreciate people kicking the tyres. If you've got a filter-heavy API or a big DataTable, try it and tell me what breaks: Package: pypi.org/project/drf-query-method ( GitHub , docs ) DRF pull request: encode/django-rest-framework#10091 drf-spectacular fix: tfranzel/drf-spectacular#1553 And if you think QUERY belongs in DRF itself (or don't), a comment on the pull request would help the maintainers see whether people actually want it. Thanks for reading!

title: A Practical First-Month SEO Plan for a New Website
author: Евгений Брусницын
summary: A new website does not need a hundred SEO tasks on day one. It needs a reliable way for people to reach important pages, content that answers actual questions, and a measurement setup that connects visits to useful actions. The first 30 days are best treated as a preparation and learning period. There is no guaranteed date by which a search engine will index every page or rank the site for a particular query. The schedule below is a practical sequence, not a promise of traffic. If you discover a serious access or tracking problem, fix it before moving on. Days 1–3: define the job and map the pages Write down what the business actually offers, who it serves, where it operates, and what a visitor should do next. A service company may want a quote request; a store may want a completed order. Make those outcomes specific enough that someone can test the journey. Create a simple page inventory with a URL or planned page, the visitor's task, publication status, owner, and next check. A small service site might begin with: A home page that explains the offer and leads to relevant services. A service page with scope, genuine conditions, and a contact path. A contact page with current details. An educational article that answers a question customers ask before they buy. Mark planned addresses separately from live ones. If a site is already public, do not rename URLs merely for aesthetics without considering existing links and a redirect plan. Check the preferred domain and protocol variants as part of the launch review. Days 4–7: verify access and crawlability Open important pages on desktop and mobile. Check whether text is readable, navigation works, buttons go where they promise, and the site loads securely. Test the contact form and trace the inquiry to the person responsible for responding. A search visit is not useful if a prospective customer cannot complete the next step. Inspect the server responses for important addresses and make sure missing pages are treated as missing rather than presented as successful pages with an error message. Check redirects and links after any corrections. Review robots.txt and page-level indexing settings with someone who understands the site. Robots.txt controls crawler access; it is not a substitute for authentication or protection of confidential information. If a page needs a noindex instruction, the crawler must be able to access the instruction to read it. Test changes on a small set of pages before applying them broadly. An XML sitemap can list the preferred, live pages that you want search engines to discover. Exclude test URLs, error pages, and unnecessary parameter variants. Submit or reference the sitemap through the relevant webmaster tools and monitor their reports. A sitemap helps communicate URLs; it does not guarantee indexing. Days 8–14: connect questions to the right pages Start with your actual products and services, customer questions, and the language people use to describe the problem. Use search research tools and any existing first-party data to refine the list. Record the source, region, and date for numerical estimates; do not invent volume or traffic forecasts when data is missing. Group similar queries by the task they express. Someone comparing air-conditioning installation prices may need a service page with clear conditions. Someone learning how to choose a unit may need an educational guide. Both topics relate to the same business, but the expected answer can differ. Create a “task → page” map. One useful page can address several closely related phrases. A separate URL for every synonym creates unnecessary maintenance. Conversely, placing every unrelated service and question on one page can make the answer hard to find. For each priority page, record what information is missing, which existing page could satisfy the task, and what the reader should do next. Treat intent as a working hypothesis to revisit when useful search data arrives. Days 15–21: make the important pages useful A service page should explain the work, the area served, meaningful limitations, and the contact process. A product page should describe current options and purchase conditions. Use actual business information rather than inventing prices, delivery promises, reviews, or case studies. Give each key page a descriptive title and a clear main heading. Write a meta description that accurately summarizes the page and distinguishes it from others. Avoid repeating a keyword unnaturally or promising a service the company does not offer. A search engine may display a different snippet, so a description is not a guarantee of what will appear in results. Use images when they add information and provide meaningful alternative text where appropriate. Select a page format based on what the visitor needs rather than a fixed word count. A useful guide, a comparison page, and a service page each have different jobs. Avoid publishing many near-identical placeholders simply to increase the page count. A smaller collection of accurate, maintainable pages is a more useful starting point for a new site. Days 22–30: connect the journey and establish measurement Make sure important pages are reachable through clear navigation and ordinary internal links. An article about choosing equipment can link to a related installation service; the service page can link to relevant questions and contact information. Link text should tell readers where they are going. Verify the site in the webmaster tools available for the search engines that matter to the audience, such as Google Search Console or Yandex Webmaster. Inspect a sample of important URLs, investigate reported problems in context, and recheck after making changes. Reports can take time to update. Configure analytics with appropriate attention to applicable data-handling requirements. Agree on the events that matter: a submitted form, a phone-link click, a checkout start, or a confirmed order. A click on a phone link is not automatically a completed call, so document what each event actually measures and avoid counting the same inquiry twice. For illustration, suppose a new site receives 100 organic visits, five form submissions, and two inquiries that meet the team's qualification criteria. These numbers are examples, not benchmarks. In a small sample, one additional inquiry changes the percentages substantially. Compare similar periods and traffic sources, and note incomplete tracking or seasonality. Day 30: a review checklist By the end of the first month, aim to answer these questions: Are the priority pages listed, owned, and assigned a visitor task? Do the site, navigation, important links, and forms work on desktop and mobile? Have crawl settings, indexing instructions, sitemap entries, and URL variants been reviewed? Is each major query group mapped to a useful page or an explicitly planned page? Are titles, descriptions, claims, contact details, and service terms accurate? Are webmaster tools and meaningful events configured, with their limitations recorded? Is there a prioritized issue list with an owner and a date for the next check? Continue after day 30: improve pages, investigate technical problems, refine internal links, and review the quality of inquiries. The first month produces a baseline and a work list; it does not finish search optimization. title: Guarding CI Pipelines with Dependency Release Age Gates
author: Alessio
summary: When an attacker compromises a package maintainer's credentials or publishes a typo-squatted package to PyPI or npm, the malicious release is immediately visible to automated tooling. Continuous integration pipelines, automated upgrade bots, and routine builds that pull the newest pinned dependencies will fetch and execute that code right away. In most cases, malicious releases are identified and yanked within a few days once security monitors and maintainers notice the compromise. However, if your automated builds pull new releases the moment they appear, your environment acts as the test bed during that dangerous early window. A dependency release age gate solves this by enforcing a cooldown period. By auditing dependency manifests and lockfiles to verify that every pinned package has existed in the public registry for a minimum number of days, you introduce a buffer period where bad releases can be caught before your build consumes them. The Problem Development workflows frequently update lockfiles through automated bots or manual upgrades. When dependencies update immediately to a release published only hours earlier, the build takes on unvetted supply chain exposure. Common threats during this early window include: Compromised developer accounts publishing malicious minor or patch updates. Fast package takeovers where existing package names are hijacked. Accidental breakages or incomplete releases that get replaced shortly after publishing. To mitigate this without completely halting updates, pipelines need an automated verification step: checking the upload timestamp of pinned dependencies against a cooldown policy. If an update is too young, the pipeline should flag it and recommend an older, verified version that meets the cooldown requirement. Install & Usage The tool is implemented as a self-contained Python script. It relies exclusively on the Python standard library, requiring no external packages from package managers. Installation Download the script file and place it in your project repository under the name depcooldown_dependency_release_age_gate.py . The script runs on standard Python. If you are running Python 3.11 or later, it uses the built-in tomllib module to read TOML files. If you run an earlier Python release, it uses an internal fallback parser to process package definitions from lockfiles. Command-Line Usage To inspect the supported command-line options: python depcooldown_dependency_release_age_gate.py --help To run an audit against a Python requirements.txt file: python depcooldown_dependency_release_age_gate.py requirements.txt You can audit an npm lockfile by passing the path to your package-lock.json : python depcooldown_dependency_release_age_gate.py package-lock.json The script can also inspect modern Python lockfiles and manifests, such as poetry.lock , uv.lock , and pyproject.toml . How It Works The tool works through three main stages: parsing manifest files, fetching upload timestamps from registries, and evaluating ages against a cutoff window. 1. Extracting Pinned Dependencies The tool inspects the structure of the input file to detect whether it belongs to the Python or npm ecosystem. It extracts package names and strictly pinned versions. Here is the implementation from parse_requirements_txt : def parse_requirements_txt ( content : str ) -> Dict [ str , str ]: """ Extract strictly pinned dependencies (name==version) from requirements.txt. """ pinned : Dict [ str , str ] = {} for raw_line in content . splitlines (): line = raw_line . strip () if not line or line . startswith ( " # " ) or line . startswith ( " - " ): continue # Strip trailing comments and environment markers if " # " in line : line = line . split ( " # " , 1 )[ 0 ]. strip () if " ; " in line : line = line . split ( " ; " , 1 )[ 0 ]. strip () # Match name[extras]==version match = re . match ( r " ^([A-Za-z0-9_.\-]+)(?:\[[^\]]*\])?\s*==\s*([A-Za-z0-9_.\-+]+)$ " , line ) if match : pkg_name = match . group ( 1 ). lower (). replace ( " _ " , " - " ) version = match . group ( 2 ). strip () pinned [ pkg_name ] = version return pinned For npm, it reads package-lock.json and extracts versions from the packages dictionary (used in modern lockfiles) or the legacy dependencies block. For Python project manifests, it reads dependencies from pyproject.toml , poetry.lock , or uv.lock . 2. Fetching Release Timestamps The RegistryClient queries public registry metadata endpoints using standard library urllib.request . For npm packages, it inspects the registry JSON metadata and reads the time object, which maps each released version to an ISO-8601 upload timestamp. For PyPI packages, it reads the releases object and extracts the upload_time_iso_8601 or upload_time entry associated with the release files. The client stores fetched metadata in an in-memory dictionary and can serialize it to a local JSON cache file to prevent redundant network lookups across runs. 3. Evaluating Cooldown Violations The audit core compares the release timestamp against the required age window: def audit_dependency ( ecosystem : str , package : str , version : str , client : RegistryClient , cooldown_days : int , reference_time : datetime . datetime , ) -> AuditResult : """ Audit a single pinned package version against the cooldown window. """ history = client . fetch_release_history ( ecosystem , package ) cutoff = reference_time - datetime . timedelta ( days = cooldown_days ) if not history or version not in history : return AuditResult ( package = package , ecosystem = ecosystem , current_version = version , upload_time = None , age_days = None , is_violation = False , suggested_version = None , reason = " Unverified (version metadata not found in registry) " , ) upload_dt = parse_iso_timestamp ( history [ version ]) age = ( reference_time - upload_dt ). total_seconds () / 86400.0 if upload_dt > cutoff : # Pinned version is in the cooldown window! Find newest safe release eligible_versions : List [ Tuple [ Tuple [ int , int , int , str ], str ]] = [] for ver_str , ts_str in history . items (): try : candidate_dt = parse_iso_timestamp ( ts_str ) if candidate_dt <= cutoff : parsed_v = parse_semver ( ver_str ) eligible_versions . append (( parsed_v , ver_str )) except Exception : continue If a package version was uploaded after the cutoff date, audit_dependency marks it as a violation. It then loops through all historical releases in the registry metadata, identifies those uploaded prior to the cutoff, sorts them using parse_semver , and returns the newest safe version as a recommendation. Limitations Before deploying the script into your automation, keep the following structural limitations in mind: Strict Pinning Requirement : The parser only evaluates exact equality pins ( == ). Flexible ranges such as >=1.2.0 , ~=2.1 , or caret dependencies in manifests are ignored unless resolved into a concrete lockfile like poetry.lock or package-lock.json . Simplified Version Parsing : Version comparison relies on parse_semver , which splits versions into major, minor, patch, and prerelease components. Complex PEP 440 specifications (such as post-releases, epoch numbers, or local versions) are parsed as zero-fallbacks or plain integers rather than strictly compliant PEP 440 objects. Minimal TOML Fallback : When running on Python versions older than 3.11 without tomllib , the script falls back to a basic line-by-line parser. While this fallback handles standard [[package]] entries in Poetry and uv lockfiles, complex or nested TOML structures may fail to parse. Registry Unavailability : If the registry metadata endpoint is unreachable, timed out, or blocked by a proxy, the tool returns an unverified status for that dependency rather than aborting. FAQ Can this tool be run in an environment without internet access? Yes. The RegistryClient supports an offline mode and local JSON cache files. If metadata was previously fetched and cached to disk, the script evaluates dependencies directly against the stored JSON cache without performing network calls. How does the script handle npm scoped packages? The script handles scoped npm packages (for example, @scope/package ) by preserving the @ character while percent-encoding the path separator when querying the npm registry endpoint. What happens if a brand-new package has no versions meeting the cooldown threshold? If a package is entirely new and none of its released versions were published before the cutoff threshold, the tool flags the pinned version as a cooldown violation and leaves the suggested version empty, indicating that no safe historical release exists in the registry. Full version and the rest of the toolkit: DepCooldown dependency release age gate on PyForge . Product page: https://py-forge.com/products/depcooldown-dependency-release-age-gate

title: Last Commit: Uncovering the Ghost in the Machine with Gemma
author: Dipanshu Raj
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Last Commit — The Ghost in the Machine 👻 What I Built Last Commit is an AI-powered GitHub investigation platform that explores repositories, gathers evidence, interprets findings, and transforms them into structured reports. Every GitHub repository has a story hidden inside it. Behind every commit, file, code change, and development decision, there are traces of what happened. Understanding those traces manually can be complicated and time-consuming. I wanted to build something that could uncover those stories. Last Commit introduces an investigation pipeline built around three major stages: Evidence: Collecting relevant information from GitHub repositories. Interpretation: Analysing and connecting collected evidence to understand what is happening. Report: Transforming findings into a structured and readable output. The platform integrates GitHub, route validation, an evidence ledger, output validation, and an AI-powered analysis layer. Why Ghost in the Machine? I interpreted the theme as exploring the hidden intelligence and forgotten traces that exist inside software systems. A repository is more than a collection of files. It contains the history of human decisions, forgotten implementations, unexplained changes, and patterns waiting to be discovered. I wanted the website itself to communicate this idea. The experience begins with an immersive, continuously rotating 3D GitHub spiral. As users scroll deeper, they travel through a mysterious digital universe filled with floating repository cards, terminal windows, code fragments, ghostly entities, spider webs, and hacker-inspired visual elements. The journey follows three central milestones: EVIDENCE → INTERPRETATION → REPORT The goal was to make repository investigation feel like exploring a mysterious digital world. Demo Live Website: https://last-commit-du3q.onrender.com GitHub Repository: https://github.com/raj-x3/last-commit/tree/master Explore the immersive interface and the GitHub investigation experience. Code GitHub Repository: https://github.com/raj-x3/last-commit The project contains the frontend, backend, GitHub integration, AI integration, evidence processing, validation mechanisms, and reporting functionality. How I Built It I approached Last Commit as a full-stack application rather than simply building an AI chatbot. The project combines: GitHub Integration: Retrieving repository-related information. AI Layer: Using Google's open-weight Gemma model to power the AI capabilities of the application. Evidence Ledger: Organising and tracking collected evidence. Route Validation: Validating investigation routes and workflow execution. Output Validation: Checking generated outputs before presenting results. Backend: Handling API requests and investigation workflows. Frontend: Providing an interactive interface and immersive 3D experience. Why Gemma? I integrated Gemma because I wanted to experiment with open-weight AI rather than make my entire project dependent on a closed proprietary model. Gemma gives developers the flexibility to work with open model weights, experiment with different inference setups, and build AI applications with greater control over their AI layer. For Last Commit, it powers the intelligence behind the investigation experience. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation matters because the future of AI should not be limited to a handful of closed ecosystems. As developers, we should have the freedom to experiment with models, understand their capabilities, customise implementations, and build applications around our own requirements. Integrating Gemma into Last Commit gave me an opportunity to explore how open-weight AI can become part of a practical software development workflow. It also makes experimentation more accessible to student developers and independent builders who want to create meaningful AI applications. I believe innovation grows faster when developers can build upon shared technology rather than starting from zero or depending entirely on closed APIs. My Agent Session The DevRelay agent session is not included in this submission. The Spirit of It There is something fascinating about looking at a repository and realising that every commit tells a small part of a much bigger story. Some changes are obvious. Others are buried deep inside files, dependencies, and development history. I wanted to build an experience that captures that feeling. The spiral represents going deeper into the machine. The terminals represent its language. The floating repositories represent its memories. And the ghostly elements represent the traces left behind by everything that once happened inside it. The machine remembers. Last Commit tries to understand what it remembers. title: I built 22 free data converters that never leave your browser (Next.js 16)
author: minh
summary: Every time I needed to turn an API response into a CSV, or paste a JSON blob out of ChatGPT into something usable, I ended up on a tool site that either wanted me to upload my data, buried the tool under 15 ads, or choked on quoted fields. So I built JSONSheet — 22 converters that run 100% in your browser . No upload. No signup. No server-side processing at all. What it does JSON ↔ CSV with proper RFC 4180 parsing (quoted fields, embedded commas/newlines, escaped quotes) JSON ↔ YAML — clean block-style output, correct quoting of ambiguous values JSON → XML and JSON → JSONL (NDJSON) for pipelines and fine-tuning datasets JSON ↔ Markdown tables — for READMEs, Notion, GitHub issues CSV/JSON → SQL INSERTs (Postgres & MySQL, with CREATE TABLE + type inference) JSON → TypeScript interfaces — nested objects become named interfaces Flatten / unflatten JSON to dot-notation paths JSON escape/unescape , Base64 encode/decode (UTF-8 safe), TSV → JSON (paste straight from Excel/Sheets), CSV dedupe & transpose , CSV → HTML table , JSON ↔ URL query string The "AI-paste" feature The part I use daily: paste JSON straight out of ChatGPT/Claude — markdown fences, "Here's your data:" prose and all — and the tool strips the noise before converting. title: Four open-source tools for AI in e-commerce, and what building them taught me
author: Naser Sadrmanesh
summary: I'm Naser Sadrmanesh, an AI product engineer and founder working on online stores. Over the last months I turned the tools I kept rebuilding for clients into four open-source projects. They are small, MIT licensed, and each one exists because a real project needed it. This post explains what each does and the design decision behind it. 1. llm-search-eval: is the new search actually better? Every store eventually changes its search: keyword to vectors, a new reranker, query rewriting, synonyms. The usual offline check is to run 50 queries, compare nDCG, and ship if the number went up. That check fails in predictable ways. Labels go stale. Gold labels were written for the old system. A new retriever surfaces products nobody labeled, so they count as misses and the new system looks worse than it is. Small deltas are noise. +2% on 50 queries is often chance. One LLM judge is one opinion. If you fill gaps with a model, someone has to check it against people. llm-search-eval builds one label pool per run: your gold labels first, LLM judgments only for the gaps, and every system scored on the same pool. You can run a panel of judges and see Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa and Krippendorff's alpha between them, plus how each judge agrees with your human labels. Every comparison gets a paired randomization test and bootstrap confidence intervals. Pairwise A/B judging runs in both orders to cancel position bias. The part teams like most is boring: an estimate command predicts the number of judge calls, tokens and cost before you run anything, and budgets stop a run before it overspends. A GitHub Action posts the result as a pull request comment and fails the check when ranking regresses. pip install llm-search-eval It has no runtime dependencies and works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including local models. There is a sample report and a live demo on Hugging Face that runs in the browser with no API keys. 2. woocommerce-mcp: let an agent touch the store, carefully The Model Context Protocol makes it easy to give an AI agent tools. For a live store, the hard question is not "can it call the API" but "what happens when it is wrong". woocommerce-mcp answers that with a few rules: Stores are read-only until you allow writes. Every write tool first returns a preview of the exact REST request. It is applied only when the tool is called again with confirm: true . Every write attempt, applied or refused, goes to an audit log . Customer data can be redacted , and tools can be allowed or denied by pattern, for example hiding delete_* . Within those rules it covers 47 tools: catalog search, orders and fulfillment with tracking, refunds, bulk price and stock changes, coupons and scheduled sales, customer segments, shipping and tax, webhooks, and sales analytics. It runs over stdio or streamable HTTP with bearer tokens or OAuth 2.0, and it is on npm, GHCR, Docker Hub and the official MCP Registry. You can browse every tool and its schema in the tool explorer . npx -y @sadrmanesh/woocommerce-mcp The lesson: the preview and confirm loop costs one extra call, and it is the single feature store owners ask about first. 3. commerce-agent-skills: teach agents the domain, not just the syntax Coding agents write plausible checkout code that misses things an experienced e-commerce engineer would never miss: idempotent webhooks, refunds that do not match the original currency unit, stock that oversells across warehouses, inaccessible product pages. commerce-agent-skills is a library of 29 skills written in plain Markdown, each with rules, reference notes, gotchas, a verification checklist and evaluation fixtures. Topics include Stripe and Iranian payment gateways, returns and refunds, inventory across warehouses, B2B pricing, catalog migration, WCAG 2.2 accessibility, Core Web Vitals, WooCommerce and Shopify development, and MCP store tooling. A small scorer checks answers against the fixtures, so a skill change can be measured instead of guessed. npx @sadrmanesh/commerce-agent-skills init The skills are tool neutral: they are just files in .agents/skills/ that any agent can read. They are also published as a Hugging Face dataset . 4. persian-rag: retrieval that respects the language Persian breaks naive pipelines quietly. Arabic and Persian Yeh and Kaf look identical but are different code points. Half-spaces come and go. Three digit systems appear in one document. PDFs often store Persian in reversed order. Common words have several accepted spellings. persian-rag handles those first, then provides a normal RAG toolkit: loaders, chunking, BM25 plus dense retrieval with rank fusion, a spelling-variant query rewriter, reranking, answers with citations resolved to source spans, chat memory, evaluation, a FastAPI server and a Docker image. The core install is pure Python with no dependencies. On its small bundled benchmark, the rewriter raises BM25 Hit@1 on misspelled queries from 0.58 to 0.83. That set is tiny, so I treat it as a regression test rather than a claim. You can try it in the live demo , and the benchmark is on Hugging Face . pip install persian-rag What ties them together All four follow the same habits: docs sites for every project, CI on every change, tagged releases that publish to PyPI, npm, GHCR, Docker Hub or the MCP Registry automatically, a GitLab mirror, and honest limits written in the README. None of them is finished. If one of them solves a problem you have, I'd be glad to hear about it, and issues and pull requests are welcome. title: LLM Text Classification: 4 JSON Schema Invariants for Reliable CRM Tags
author: JorisRhodes8286
summary: Use JSON Schema when an LLM's classification result becomes a CRM action. Keep prompt parsing for disposable analysis, prototypes, and human-reviewed notes. The distinction is not about making the model “understand JSON.” It is about placing a checkable contract between uncertain text generation and a system that will create a task, change a field, or trigger an escalation. For a logistics sales call, I would require four invariants before accepting a result: a closed set of labels, the right value types, required fields, and an explicit representation for uncertainty. Then I would validate the response, reject or quarantine failures, and only after that map it into CRM commands. A regular expression around a prompt-shaped answer cannot provide that boundary reliably. Should I use JSON Schema for structured LLM output? The input might be a transcript in which a shipper asks about a lane, a delivery window, and a quote. The useful output is not a paragraph. It is a small record that another process can inspect: classification = { " intent " : " quote_request " , " urgency " : " normal " , " follow_up_required " : True , " confidence " : 0.86 , " evidence " : " The shipper asked for a quote on the Chicago-to-Dallas lane. " } The schema is the decision record. It says what values are legal and which fields are mandatory. A JSON parser answers one narrow question: “Can these characters be decoded as JSON?” That is useful, but it does not answer whether urgency is a permitted value, whether confidence is a number, or whether the record contains the fields needed by the CRM workflow. Prompt parsing usually starts with an instruction such as “return intent | urgency | next step .” The parser then splits on a delimiter, trims whitespace, and hopes the model follows the layout. One extra sentence, a translated label, or a delimiter inside the evidence can move every value into the wrong column. The result may still look plausible to a reader. That is the dangerous case. The four invariants create separate failure boundaries: Invariant Example rule Failure response Vocabulary intent is one of a finite set Quarantine for review Type confidence is a number from 0 to 1 Reject the record Presence follow_up_required is required Reject the record Uncertainty confidence and evidence travel with the label Route low-confidence work differently These rules do not make a classification correct. They make malformed and out-of-contract classifications visible. That difference matters when an automated tag becomes a sales task. That is the boundary. Consider a call where the shipper says, “The delivery is late, but I also need a quote for next month.” A single-label classifier has a domain decision to make; a parser has a string decision to make. If the response contains service_issue first and quote_request second, a delimiter-based consumer may silently keep the first value. A schema can reject an array when the contract expects one intent, but the team still has to decide whether to add multi-intent support, choose a primary intent, or send the call to review. The validation failure is useful because it puts that domain choice in front of the owner instead of burying it in a split function. Why is prompt parsing a weak boundary? A prompt is an instruction, not a type system. It can improve the distribution of likely answers, but a downstream service still needs to establish what it received. Delimiter parsing adds another grammar whose edge cases are easy to underestimate: missing columns, repeated separators, an empty value, a quoted separator, or an answer wrapped in explanatory prose. Do not guess. I started by thinking a short pipe-delimited format would be easier for a small classifier. Later I found the real cost was not splitting the string; it was deciding what to do when the split produced five fields, when a label had a different spelling, or when an apparently numeric score was high . The parser had quietly become a second, undocumented schema. It was harder to review than a declared contract. There is also a retry problem. If parsing fails, should the application resend the same transcript, ask for a shorter answer, or treat the call as unclassified? Those choices affect duplicate CRM tasks and audit history. A schema-backed pipeline can record the exact validation error and preserve the original response. A prompt parser often turns all of these cases into a generic “parse failed” branch. This is why structured output should be treated as a boundary in the application, not as a formatting preference in the prompt. The model remains probabilistic. The consumer becomes deterministic about what it will accept. Which architecture keeps the failure contained? The critical path is deliberately boring: classify, validate, normalize only where the contract allows it, then perform a side effect. Validation must happen before a CRM write, and the original model response should remain available for diagnosis without being mistaken for trusted data. from json import loads from jsonschema import ValidationError , validate CLASSIFICATION_SCHEMA = { " type " : " object " , " required " : [ " intent " , " urgency " , " follow_up_required " , " confidence " , " evidence " ], " additionalProperties " : False , " properties " : { " intent " : { " type " : " string " , " enum " : [ " quote_request " , " status_question " , " service_issue " , " other " ], }, " urgency " : { " type " : " string " , " enum " : [ " low " , " normal " , " high " ]}, " follow_up_required " : { " type " : " boolean " }, " confidence " : { " type " : " number " , " minimum " : 0 , " maximum " : 1 }, " evidence " : { " type " : " string " , " minLength " : 1 }, }, } def classify_call ( transcript : str ) -> dict : raw_text = call_classifier ( transcript ) try : result = loads ( raw_text ) validate ( instance = result , schema = CLASSIFICATION_SCHEMA ) except ( ValueError , ValidationError ) as error : store_for_review ( transcript = transcript , raw_response = raw_text , reason = str ( error )) raise UnclassifiedCall from error if result [ " confidence " ] < 0.70 : store_for_review ( transcript = transcript , raw_response = raw_text , reason = " low confidence " ) return result crm_action = to_crm_action ( result ) write_crm_action ( crm_action ) return result The endpoint names in this example are intentionally generic. The important properties are ordering and ownership. call_classifier produces an untrusted string. validate establishes the contract. to_crm_action is the only place that translates a classification into a side effect. A low-confidence result can remain visible without being allowed to create an automatic follow-up. In production, I would also give each transcript an idempotency key. A retry after a timeout must not create two “call shipper” tasks merely because the first write was uncertain. That key is an application concern, separate from JSON Schema, but structured output makes the boundary explicit enough to test. The schema itself deserves change control. Adding a new intent is a data migration for dashboards and routing rules, even if it looks like one line of JSON. Version the contract, keep fixtures for every accepted label, and include malformed responses in the test suite. Test the negative space: missing evidence, an unknown intent, a string confidence, an extra property, and a valid record with a low score. The audit record should make a failed attempt reconstructable without making the transcript broadly visible: keep the contract version, the validation error, the raw response in an access-controlled store, the retry decision, and the eventual human disposition. If a timeout occurs after validation but before the CRM write, the idempotency key should let the writer check for an existing action before retrying. If the classifier is called again after a schema change, retain both schema versions so an analyst can explain why the same transcript produced different routing. This is more storage and operational discipline than a delimiter parser needs, but it is the discipline required when a tag controls work. What should the decision record reject? I would reject “parse whatever the prompt returns” for automated CRM actions. It optimizes for a quick first demo and pushes complexity into hidden coercions: converting yes to true , mapping urgent to high , or silently dropping an unrecognized field. Those coercions make dashboards look clean while weakening the audit trail. The rejected option is still valid in two situations. First, a human is reading the output and no machine action depends on its shape. Second, the output is exploratory material that will be thrown away after analysis. In both cases, the application can tolerate more variation because a person or a later explicit step owns the interpretation. A schema is not a substitute for domain review. other may be valid syntactically and still useless operationally. A confidence value may be well-formed without being calibrated. The contract should therefore capture evidence and route ambiguous records to a queue whose service level the team has agreed on. Do not promote every valid object to an automated decision. The trade-off is real: a schema adds design work, validation code, fixtures, and a migration decision whenever the label set changes. It can also reject a response that contains useful information in an unexpected shape. That cost is justified for a CRM write, where a false task or incorrect tag is durable operational data. It is unnecessary overhead for a scratchpad summary that a person will read and discard. This approach is also a poor fit when the output is inherently open-ended, such as a long narrative for an analyst. In that case, constrain only the metadata that downstream systems need and leave the prose free-form. Forcing every sentence into a closed schema can make the interface less useful without improving the decision. How do you know the contract is working? Measure rejected records by reason, not only by overall success rate. A spike in unknown intents can mean the label set is stale. A spike in missing fields can mean a prompt or runtime change. A spike in low-confidence classifications can indicate transcript quality, a new call pattern, or a decision boundary that needs review. Keep the raw transcript access-controlled because sales calls can contain personal and commercial information. Store the schema version, validation result, model response metadata that your runtime exposes, and the final CRM action together in an audit record. Redact or minimize transcript content in ordinary logs. Delivery and retention policies belong in the system design; they should not be improvised inside an exception handler. The practical rule is short: use a schema when another system must trust the shape, and use prompt parsing only when a human or a disposable experiment can absorb the ambiguity. For logistics call tagging, that boundary is the difference between a useful classification and an automated CRM mistake that looks like clean data. References JSON Schema, “JSON Schema Specification”: https://json-schema.org/specification JSON Schema, “Understanding JSON Schema”: https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema RFC 8259, “The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259 AWS, “Amazon Bedrock”: https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/

title: Canada Joins EuroHPC: What the EU Compute Partnership Could Mean for AI Access
